extracted.intended_audience: industrialists, managers, entrepreneurs and students of manufacturing/steel industry business practice
extracted.subtask_description: Practical business rules and standards for running and expanding a 19th-century steel/manufacturing concern, including raw-material strategy, plant acquisition, mine examination, corporate structure, and policies for labor disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity for owning raw materials and finishing the completed article
rubrics_metrics.description: The one vital lesson in iron and steel: the necessity for owning raw materials and finishing the completed article ready for its purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After solving the steel-rail problem, the next step was erecting blast furnaces; later the firm acquired coke supplies and iron stone so that it could make finished steel products rather than remain dependent on suppliers. Owning raw materials and finishing plants is presented as central to independence and success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid purchases of inferior plants
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing so unsatisfactory as purchases of inferior plants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie recounts purchasing a reconstructed blast furnace that cost as much as a new one and 'never was as good.' Even if a bad purchase later yields unexpected uses, the direct lesson is to avoid buying inferior or misrepresented plants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop internal supply chain (blast furnaces, coke, iron stone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Independence requires control of blast-furnace capacity, supply of superior coke, and access to iron stone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Built blast furnaces, purchased half then majority stock in the Frick Coke Company for fuel supply, and sought ironstone mines; plant-by-plant improvements raised capacity massively. The chain components (ore, coal/coke, limestone, furnaces) and logistics are emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough geological and assay investigation before buying mineral property
rubrics_metrics.description: Every purchaser of mineral property should make the examination most carefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical procedure given: run lines across a hillside fifty feet apart with cross-lines one hundred feet apart; at each intersection put a shaft and analyze ore at every few feet of depth — example: eighty shafts and frequent assays to know 'exactly what there was of ore' before paying the price.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partnerships enable faster opportunistic action than corporations
rubrics_metrics.description: Partnerships have the great advantage of speed in seizing opportunities compared with corporations required to consult boards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie notes that had a corporation needed board approval for a mine purchase, 'by that time the mine would probably have become the property of others.' Use partnerships when rapid decisions matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound rule: give money freely when you have a surplus, but never your name
rubrics_metrics.description: You may give money freely when you have a surplus, but your name never—neither as endorser nor as member of a corporation with individual liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A small investment or having your name on the shareholder list with individual liability can be 'a trifle possessed of deadly explosive power'—example: twenty shares in a failing bank nearly imperiled credit. Avoid personal guarantees and membership in concerns with individual liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquire only after confirming sufficient ore in sight to repay investment
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not pay for mineral property until analyses show there is enough ore in sight to repay the purchase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After methodical shafting and assays, Carnegie was satisfied the Scotia ore justified the hundred thousand dollar purchase; thorough confirmation reduces investment losses experienced elsewhere (e.g., Tyrone region).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use chemists and laboratory analysis as guides for mining and smelting decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The chemist as guide: use laboratory analyses to identify suitable ores and to inform purchases and production choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chemist Prousser's analyses found ore low in phosphorus suitable for Bessemer steel; the chemist's role included analyzing numerous specimens and encouraging locals to bring samples. Even if the chemist required social convincing, his technical judgment proved decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: When purchasing other works, propose consolidation on equal terms (dollar-for-dollar equality)
rubrics_metrics.description: A fair consolidation offer is to propose equality so every dollar invested by the sellers ranks against your dollars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie's approach to buying Homestead mills was to propose consolidation with every dollar they had invested to rank against Carnegie's dollars; giving parties the option to take cash eased negotiations and prevented feeling overreached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horizontal integration and diversification of finishing capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Expand capacity to make almost everything from small to large steel products to capture more of the value chain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishing Hartman Steel Works to work Homestead output into a hundred various forms allowed the firm to make everything from a wire nail up to a twenty-inch girder, reducing dependence on outside finishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous plant improvement and expansion — decay begins when a concern stops extending
rubrics_metrics.description: A manufacturing concern in a growing country begins to decay when it stops extending; continually improve each new plant upon the preceding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie describes successive improvements in blast-furnace plants and tripling of capacities over a decade; he frames expansion and modernization as axiomatic to long-term survival.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of the Surplus: rely on best home market and export surplus
rubrics_metrics.description: A nation with the best home market and standardized products can depend on returns from home sales and export surplus profitably; this is the 'Law of the Surplus.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if export prices only cover actual cost, charging exports with their proportion of expenses enables profitable overseas sales; standardization of product aids competitiveness abroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt new technologies and invest to modernize when existing machinery becomes obsolete
rubrics_metrics.description: When machinery becomes obsolete (e.g., Bessemer, open-hearth, basic processes), invest millions to reconstruct and enlarge works to achieve higher productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New machinery produced about sixty percent more steel than the old; though adoption can create labor tensions, failing to modernize risks competitive disadvantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair sharing of productivity gains as a labor-management policy
rubrics_metrics.description: When productivity increases from new machinery, propose to divide the gains between the men and the firm (example: divide a 60% gain into 30% to men and 30% to firm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The firm offered a scale that would give the men thirty percent more than under the old scale, leaving thirty percent to recompense the firm for its outlay. Presented as fair and generous under ordinary circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refuse unreasonable or extortionate labor demands
rubrics_metrics.description: A firm should not accede to attempts to extort the whole of productivity gains from management simply because of external pressure or contracts obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie recounts the union leaders demanding the whole 60% gain; firm refused because it was unreasonable and because of existing urgent contracts (e.g., government armor) and obligations (Chicago Exhibition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Labor-dispute policy: confer freely, wait patiently, and do not employ new men to replace strikers
rubrics_metrics.description: The company's rule: be known as determined to let the men at any works stop work; confer freely with them and wait patiently until they decide to return to work; never attempt to employ new men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie argues that the best workmen are not idle and that replacing skilled men is impractical for complex modern steel plants; employing new men turns neutral workers into lukewarm opponents and resents the practice—hence the firm should avoid it except perhaps to test a promise to return.

rubrics_metrics.name: When testing whether non-union workers will run works, make them responsible for their own protection
rubrics_metrics.description: If inviting non-union men to run the works, make it their responsibility to protect themselves rather than provide armed protection that reverses responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of stationing sheriff guards to protect thousands against hundreds, the company might tell the three thousand men: 'if you will come and run the works without protection'—thus shifting responsibility to them. Opening works with external protection can backfire by seeming to use force against strikers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of political and public relations consequences of labor conflicts and seek rehabilitation via dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Public perception of violence at company works can tarnish reputation; seek vindication through civic engagement and dialogue with labor federations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie describes being perceived as responsible for Homestead violence, then being reconciled through involvement with the National Civic Federation and personal outreach (dinner with officials, addressing mass meeting) that restored relations and mitigated reputational harm.
